chunks: Muhammad, from Ahmad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam and Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-Ala ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two (peace be upon them both), who said:
I asked him about the child whom the man emancipates. So he said: Yes, Ali (peace be upon him) had emancipated numerous children.

key_terms.أعتق: A'taqa — he emancipated, freed from slavery; the act of manumission
key_terms.الصبي: Sabiyy — a young child, minor; in fiqh contexts refers to a pre-pubescent slave
key_terms.وِلْدَان: Wildan — children, youths; plural of walad (child/offspring)
key_terms.يعتقه: Yu'tiquhu — to emancipate, to grant freedom from slavery; from 'atq (manumission)

ai.seo_question: Can a man emancipate an enslaved child in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Muhammad ibn Muslim asked the Imam — either al-Baqir or al-Sadiq (peace be upon them) — whether a man may lawfully emancipate an enslaved child. The Imam affirmed the permissibility by citing the precedent of Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), who had emancipated many children during his caliphate. This narration establishes a legal ruling in Shia fiqh that emancipating minors is valid, grounding the ruling in the practice of the first Imam.
